# docs/configuration/README.md

# YAML Configuration Guide

**Everything you need to know about writing kaboo-workflows YAML configs — from zero to production.**

kaboo-workflows lets you describe entire multi-agent systems in YAML and get back live, fully wired strands objects. This guide walks you through every configuration option, from the simplest one-agent setup to nested multi-orchestration systems with MCP servers, hooks, session persistence, conditional graph pipelines, and multi-file configs.

No prior YAML expertise required. We start simple and build up.

---

## Table of Contents

1. [The Basics — Your First Config](Chapter_01.md)
2. [Models — Choosing Your LLM](Chapter_02.md)
3. [Variables — Environment-Driven Config](Chapter_03.md)
4. [YAML Anchors — DRY Config Blocks](Chapter_04.md)
5. [Tools — Giving Agents Superpowers](Chapter_05.md)
6. [Hooks — Middleware for Agents](Chapter_06.md)
7. [Session Persistence — Memory That Survives Restarts](Chapter_07.md)
8. [Conversation Managers — Controlling Context Windows](Chapter_08.md)
9. [MCP — External Tool Servers](Chapter_09.md)
10. [Orchestrations — Multi-Agent Systems](Chapter_10.md)
11. [Graph Conditions — Dynamic Routing](Chapter_11.md)
12. [Nested Orchestrations — Composing Systems](Chapter_12.md)
13. [Multi-File Configs — Splitting and Merging](Chapter_13.md)
14. [Agent Factories — Custom Agent Construction](Chapter_14.md)
15. [Event Streaming — Real-Time Observability](Chapter_15.md)
16. [Name Sanitization — How Names Are Handled](Chapter_16.md)
17. [The Loading Pipeline — What Happens Under the Hood](Chapter_17.md)
18. [Full Reference — Every Field at a Glance](Chapter_18.md)
19. [Attachments & Multimodal — References for Every Agent](Chapter_19.md)

**Bonus**: [Quick Recipes](Quick_Recipes.md) — Copy-paste-ready configs for common patterns.

---

That covers everything kaboo-workflows YAML has to offer. When in doubt, check the [examples](https://github.com/gl-pgege/kaboo-workflows/tree/main/examples) — each one is a self-contained demo of the concepts above. And remember: after `load()`, what you get back are plain strands objects. No wrappers, no subclasses. Just the real deal, fully wired and ready to go.

Happy composing! 🎼

# docs/evaluation.md

# Evaluation

kaboo-workflows treats evaluation as a first-class, opt-in feature with two
loops:

- **Online**: live runs emit OpenTelemetry traces (agent → cycle → model →
  tool spans, with tokens and cost) to any OTLP backend. User feedback from the
  UI attaches scores to the exact trace.
- **Offline**: a golden dataset of real questions runs headlessly through the
  *same* wire path as production, and pluggable scorers gate the result with a
  nonzero exit code.

Everything is off by default and zero-overhead when disabled: with telemetry
off, no OTel SDK is configured and all instrumentation is a no-op.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph online [Online loop]
        Run[Live workflow run] -->|OTel spans| Hub[(OTLP backend, e.g. Langfuse)]
        UI[kaboo-react TurnFeedback] -->|"score {traceId, value}"| Host[Host backend]
        Host -->|create_score| Hub
    end
    subgraph offline [Offline loop]
        Golden[Golden dataset YAML/JSONL] --> Runner[kaboo-workflows eval]
        Runner -->|headless runs| Scores[Scorers]
        Scores -->|report + exit code| Gate[CLI / pytest]
        Scores -->|optional push| Hub
    end
    Hub -->|bad traces promoted| Golden
```

## Online tracing

### Enable telemetry

Add a `telemetry` section to your config:

```yaml
telemetry:
  enabled: true
  service_name: my-agent-service     # OTel service.name (default: kaboo-workflows)
  otlp:
    endpoint: http://localhost:3010/api/public/otel   # traces go to <endpoint>/v1/traces
    headers:                          # or a single "k=v,k2=v2" string
      Authorization: Basic <base64(public:secret)>
      x-langfuse-ingestion-version: "4"
  sample_ratio: 1.0                   # 0..1, trace-id ratio sampling
  console: false                      # also print spans to stdout (debugging)
  trace_attributes:                   # static attributes stamped on every span
    deployment.environment: local
```

Or via environment variables (no config change needed):

| Variable | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `KABOO_TELEMETRY_ENABLED` | `true`/`false` — overrides `telemetry.enabled` in *both* directions (kill switch) |
| `KABOO_OTLP_ENDPOINT` or `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` | OTLP base endpoint |
| `KABOO_OTLP_HEADERS` or `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS` | `k=v,k2=v2` header string |

When enabled, kaboo initializes strands' `StrandsTelemetry` (agent, cycle,
model, and tool spans following the GenAI semantic conventions) with a batch
span processor — spans stream out incrementally, nothing buffers per run.
Initialization is process-wide and idempotent; an existing global
`TracerProvider` is respected.

### Conversation attributes

Every span is stamped with the identifiers kaboo already tracks, so traces
correlate 1:1 with what the UI shows:

| Attribute | Source |
| --- | --- |
| `session.id` | AG-UI `threadId` |
| `user.id` | authenticated principal (`sub`/`username` claim), when auth is on |
| `kaboo.run.id` | AG-UI `runId` |
| `kaboo.turn.id` | kaboo's logical turn id (stable across interrupt/resume) |

### Trace id in the event stream

The active trace id rides outward so hosts can attach scores to the exact
trace:

- `AGENT_COMPLETE` events carry `trace_id`;
- `RUN_FINISHED.metadata.traceId` names the run's root trace, and each
  sub-agent's `SUBAGENT_STARTED.metadata.traceId` its own (kaboo-react's
  `ActivityState.traceByRun` / `StreamGroup.traceId`);
- `current_trace_id()` (exported from `kaboo_workflows`) returns the ambient
  trace id, `None` when telemetry is off.

### Langfuse quickstart (reference backend)

Any OTLP backend works; [Langfuse](https://langfuse.com) is the reference
because it adds score APIs, LLM-as-judge evaluators, and annotation queues on
top of the traces. Self-hosted:

1. Run Langfuse v4 (web + worker + ClickHouse + MinIO + Redis, reusing your
   Postgres with a dedicated `langfuse` database).
2. Create an org/project and an API key pair in the UI.
3. Point telemetry at it:

```bash
KABOO_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:3010/api/public/otel
KABOO_OTLP_HEADERS="Authorization=Basic $(echo -n pk-lf-…:sk-lf-… | base64),x-langfuse-ingestion-version=4"
KABOO_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=true
```

Traces appear under the project within seconds of a run; `session.id` groups
them per conversation.

### User feedback

kaboo-react ships a `TurnFeedback` component / `useTurnFeedback` hook that
resolves the turn's `traceId` and calls a host-provided `onFeedback` callback
— the library stores nothing. The host backend forwards the payload to the
backend's score API (for Langfuse: `create_score(trace_id=…,
name="user-feedback", value=…)`). See the kaboo-react feedback guide.

## Offline evals

Install the extras you need:

```bash
pip install 'kaboo-workflows[evals]'                 # jsonschema for json_schema scorer
pip install 'kaboo-workflows[evals,eval-deepeval]'   # + DeepEval metrics
pip install 'kaboo-workflows[evals,langfuse]'        # + push experiments to Langfuse
```

### Golden dataset format

YAML (or JSONL, one item per line):

```yaml
name: golden-v1                # dataset name (defaults to the file stem)
config: ./config.yaml          # workflow config, relative to this file
scorers:                       # applied to every item
  - type: budget
    max_cost: 2.0
    max_latency_s: 300
items:
  - id: revenue-q3
    input: "What was total revenue in Q3?"
    expect:                    # item-specific scorers
      - type: contains
        value: ["revenue", "Q3"]
      - type: tool_called
        tool: run_sql
      - type: judge
        rubric: "States the Q3 revenue figure with the currency and cites the source table."
  - id: chart
    input: "Plot monthly signups for 2025"
    expect:
      - type: trajectory
        tools: [sql_analyst, chart_visualizer]
```

Item fields: `id` (defaults to `item-<index>`), `input` (required),
`expect`, `state`, `forwarded_props`, `timeout_s` (default 600),
`metadata`.

Every item is implicitly checked by `run_succeeded` (the run finished without
an error) before any configured scorer.

### Built-in scorers

| Type | Checks | Keys |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `contains` / `not_contains` | substring(s) in the final text | `value`, `case_sensitive` |
| `regex` | pattern matches the final text | `pattern`, `flags` (`imsx`) |
| `tool_called` | a tool ran | `tool`, `agent`, `min_count` |
| `trajectory` | tools appear in order (subsequence) | `tools` |
| `budget` | cost / latency / token caps | `max_cost`, `max_latency_s`, `max_input_tokens`, `max_output_tokens`, `max_total_tokens` |
| `json_schema` | structured output (or text-as-JSON) validates | `schema` |
| `judge` | LLM-as-judge against a rubric | `rubric`, `model`, `threshold` (default 0.7), `name` |
| `deepeval` | any DeepEval metric | `metric`, `threshold`, metric kwargs |

The trajectory includes sub-agent invocations: a delegation or handoff to
`sql_analyst` counts as a step named `sql_analyst`, followed by that agent's
own tool calls — so `trajectory` and `tool_called` work across orchestration
modes.

The `judge` scorer resolves its model from the workflow config's own
`models:` section (`model: sonnet-4-5`), or takes an inline mapping
(`model: {provider: openai, model_id: …}`). Judges see the user input, the
final answer, and the tool trajectory, and return a 0–1 score with reasoning.

Custom scorers plug in via the same import-spec mechanism as model providers:

```yaml
expect:
  - type: my_pkg.scoring:GroundednessScorer   # or ./scorers.py:ClassName
    some_kwarg: 42
```

The class needs a `name` attribute and an
`async def score(item, capture) -> ScoreResult` method. The `capture`
(`RunCapture`) exposes `text`, `tools` (with per-agent attribution),
`structured_outputs`, `usage` (tokens + cost), `latency_s`, `groups`, and
`error`.

### Running

```bash
kaboo-workflows eval datasets/golden.yaml                     # all items
kaboo-workflows eval datasets/golden.yaml --item revenue-q3   # subset (repeatable)
kaboo-workflows eval datasets/golden.yaml --max-items 5
kaboo-workflows eval datasets/golden.yaml --output results.jsonl
kaboo-workflows eval datasets/golden.yaml --config overrides.yaml
kaboo-workflows eval datasets/golden.yaml --push-langfuse     # upload as a dataset experiment
```

Each item runs headlessly through the production wire path — the same agents,
orchestrations, MCP tools, and hooks your service uses — one at a time, with
per-item progress and a summary table. The exit code is nonzero when any
scorer fails, so the command gates CI as-is.

`--push-langfuse` uploads the items to a Langfuse dataset (idempotent by item
id) and records the run as an experiment with every scorer verdict attached
as a score. Requires the `langfuse` extra plus `LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY`,
`LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY`, and `LANGFUSE_BASE_URL` (or `LANGFUSE_HOST`).

### From Python / pytest

```python
from kaboo_workflows.evals import assert_eval, run_eval

async def test_golden_dataset():
    report = await run_eval("datasets/golden.yaml")
    assert_eval(report)   # raises AssertionError with the summary on failure
```

`run_eval` also accepts `config=`, `item_ids=`, `max_items=`, `output=`, and
an `on_item=` progress callback; the returned `EvalReport` exposes `ok`,
`failed`, `total_cost`, `summary()`, and `to_dict()`.

### DeepEval metrics

With the `eval-deepeval` extra, any DeepEval metric wraps into a scorer:

```yaml
expect:
  - type: deepeval
    metric: deepeval.metrics:AnswerRelevancyMetric
    threshold: 0.8
```

## Scale and toggle guarantees

- **Off by default** — no OTel SDK configured means every instrumentation
  point is a no-op; `KABOO_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false` force-disables even a
  config that says `enabled: true`.
- **Any pipeline size** — spans export through batch processors, the eval
  runner streams items one at a time and appends each JSONL line as it
  completes; nothing buffers a whole run in memory.
- **No vendor lock-in** — the library speaks OTLP and a thin scorer protocol;
  Langfuse, Phoenix, or a bare collector are config swaps.

# docs/getting-started.md

# Getting started

This page takes you from an empty directory to a running multi-agent server in
a few minutes. Every snippet here is exercised in CI.

!!! note "Compatibility"
    kaboo-workflows requires **Python 3.12+** and is built on
    [strands-agents](https://github.com/strands-agents/harness-sdk). Model
    provider SDKs are optional extras (`openai`, `ollama`, `gemini`,
    `agentcore-memory`) — install the one you need.

## 1. Install

```bash
pip install "kaboo-workflows[openai]"
# or with uv
uv add "kaboo-workflows[openai]"
```

## 2. Write a config

The whole system is a single YAML file: models, agents, tools, and the `entry`
point. Save this as `config.yaml`:

```yaml
vars:
  OPENROUTER_API_KEY: ${OPENROUTER_API_KEY}

models:
  default:
    provider: openai
    model_id: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4
    params:
      client_args:
        base_url: https://openrouter.ai/api/v1
        api_key: ${OPENROUTER_API_KEY}

agents:
  assistant:
    model: default
    system_prompt: "You are a helpful assistant."

entry: assistant
```

`${VAR}` interpolates from the environment (see
[Chapter 1](configuration/Chapter_01.md)), so no secrets live in the file.

## 3a. Serve it (AG-UI SSE)

`kaboo-serve` resolves the config and serves your agents as AG-UI
Server-Sent Events that any [CopilotKit](https://copilotkit.ai) frontend can
consume:

```bash
OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-... uv run kaboo-serve config.yaml
```

The server listens on `http://localhost:8080` — `POST /invocations` for the
event stream and `GET /ping` for health.

## 3b. Or drive it from Python

`load()` hands back live, fully wired `strands` objects. There are no wrappers:
`resolved.entry` is a real `strands.Agent` (or a `Swarm`/`Graph` for
orchestrations), so you call it directly.

```{.python notest}
from kaboo_workflows import load

resolved = load("config.yaml")
agent = resolved.entry              # a plain strands.Agent
try:
    agent("What is 15 * 23?")       # streams the reply to stdout
finally:
    resolved.mcp_lifecycle.stop()   # always release MCP servers/clients
```

Wrap CLI-style entrypoints in `cli_errors()` for friendly error messages:

```{.python notest}
from kaboo_workflows import cli_errors, load

with cli_errors():
    resolved = load("config.yaml")
    resolved.entry("Hello!")
```

## Next steps

- **[Concepts](concepts.md)** — the mental model behind `load()` and serving.
- **[Configuration reference](configuration/README.md)** — every YAML option,
  chapter by chapter.
- **[Workflows](workflows/deep-nesting.md)** — worked, tested multi-agent
  patterns (delegate, swarm, graph, parallel, HITL).
- **[Examples](https://github.com/gl-pgege/kaboo-workflows/tree/main/examples)** —
  ~20 self-contained, load-tested example projects.
- **[Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md)** — fixes for the common first-run
  errors.

# docs/index.md

# kaboo-workflows

**YAML-driven multi-agent orchestration with AG-UI and CopilotKit support, built
on [strands-agents](https://github.com/strands-agents/harness-sdk).**

Describe an entire multi-agent system in YAML — models, agents, tools, hooks, MCP
servers, and nested orchestrations — and `load()` hands back live, fully wired
strands objects. `kaboo-serve` then serves them as AG-UI Server-Sent Events that
any [CopilotKit](https://copilotkit.ai) frontend can consume.

  or drive it from Python in a few minutes.

## The kaboo stack

kaboo-workflows is the orchestration engine. It pairs with:

- **[kaboo-runtime](https://github.com/gl-pgege/kaboo-runtime)** — a CopilotKit
  runtime plugin for persisting and replaying agent event logs (in-memory or
  Postgres `ThreadStore`s).
- **[kaboo-react](https://github.com/gl-pgege/kaboo-react)** — React components
  for rendering agent activity.
- **[kaboo-workflows-demo](https://github.com/gl-pgege/kaboo-workflows-demo)** —
  a runnable, end-to-end reference wiring all three together.

See [the kaboo stack](https://gl-pgege.github.io/kaboo-docs/) for the whole
picture.

## Everything is proven

Nothing documented here ships without a test: every example config is
load-validated, every complex workflow guide is backed by a passing end-to-end
test, executable doc snippets run in CI, and a completeness gate guarantees every
public symbol has a docstring and an API page.

# docs/recipes/asking-the-user.md

# Ask the user, and request inputs

An agent that guesses when it should ask produces confident wrong answers. A
question, a file upload or a choice of data source is a tool the browser runs:
the client declares it with each run, the agent calls it, the run waits, and the
person's answer goes back to the agent that asked
([Human-in-the-loop](../workflows/human-in-the-loop.md) has the protocol). The
server needs no code for it, only an allow-list.

## The agent side

```yaml
agents:
  assistant:
    client_tools: [ask_user, request_files, request_datasources]
    system_prompt: |
      When the question is ambiguous, ask once with ask_user, putting every
      open question into that one call with a few options each. When the data
      you need is not attached, call request_datasources rather than asking in
      prose.
```

`client_tools` names the browser's tools this agent may call. Any agent may
have one, delegates included, and an agent never sees a browser tool its list
doesn't name. Questions are usually best from one voice — the agent the person
talks to — but an analyst deep in a delegate can ask too: its question shows in
the main chat under its name, and its coordinator is told what was asked and
answered.

## The browser side

The client declares each tool, with its description and schema, and draws what
the person answers. With kaboo-react:

```tsx
import { useAskUserTool, useRequestTool } from "@pgege/kaboo-react";

function BrowserTools() {
  useAskUserTool();
  useRequestTool({
    name: "request_datasources",
    description: "Ask the person to pick data sources and wait for the choice.",
    parameters: RequestDatasourcesArgs,
    render: DatasourcesPanel,
  });
  return null;
}
```

- **`ask_user`** asks multiple-choice questions: two or more options each,
  `multiple` for multi-select, and an **Other** choice for an answer in the
  person's own words. The answer is a `{question: answer}` map.
- **A request** is any other input. Its panel calls `answer` with what the
  model should read; `skip` tells the model the person declined.
- **Arguments are checked** against the tool's schema. A malformed call is
  answered with an error that names the problem, so the model corrects it
  instead of the person seeing a broken panel.
- **Several requests show in order**: one agent's questions as one card, and
  several agents' requests one after another.

## What the user experiences

- The run pauses; the chat shows the card or panel; the answer resumes the
  agent that asked, mid-thought, rather than starting over.
- There is no time limit. The paused agent travels in the conversation's state,
  so the person can close the browser, come back days later on another device,
  and answer; it also survives a restart or a second replica
  ([A pause outlives the process](../workflows/human-in-the-loop.md#a-pause-outlives-the-process-that-opened-it)).
- If the person sends a message instead of answering, the request is skipped
  and the agent answers the message
  ([The person can move on](../workflows/human-in-the-loop.md#the-person-can-move-on)).

## A request that needs the server

When answering a request takes server logic — checking the person may use a
data source, say — make it a server tool that interrupts. Declare it with
`context=True` and call `tool_context.interrupt` with a reason whose `type`
names your kind. Whatever the client sends back on resume becomes the
interrupt's return value:

```python
import json
from typing import Any

from strands import tool
from strands.types.tools import ToolContext


def _answer(response: Any) -> str:
    if isinstance(response, dict) and response.get("status") == "cancelled":
        return "The user skipped the request."
    return json.dumps(response, ensure_ascii=False)


@tool(name="pick_account", context=True)
def pick_account(tool_context: ToolContext, reason: str) -> dict:
    """Pause and ask the user to pick one of their billing accounts.

    Args:
        reason: Why an account is needed, shown to the user.
    """
    response = tool_context.interrupt(name="pick_account", reason={"type": "account", "message": reason})
    return {"status": "success", "content": [{"text": _answer(response)}]}
```

kaboo-react renders the interrupt with the component registered for its type
(`interruptRenderers={{ account: AccountPicker }}`), and shows a minimal card
with the `message` and Skip wherever nothing is registered.

## Test it

A scripted model can call a browser tool, and `Pipeline.turn(tools=..., messages=...)`
answers it the way a browser does ([Testing](../testing.md#browser-tools-approvals-and-resume)).
Lab scenarios:
[question-several](https://github.com/gl-pgege/kaboo-docs/blob/main/examples/kaboo-workflows-demo/scenarios/question-several.yaml),
[question-subagent](https://github.com/gl-pgege/kaboo-docs/blob/main/examples/kaboo-workflows-demo/scenarios/question-subagent.yaml)
and
[request-datasources](https://github.com/gl-pgege/kaboo-docs/blob/main/examples/kaboo-workflows-demo/scenarios/request-datasources.yaml).

# docs/recipes/attachments-and-images.md

# Images and file attachments

Users attach spreadsheets, PDFs and screenshots; tools produce images worth
looking at. [Chapter 19](../configuration/Chapter_19.md) documents every knob.
This recipe is the setup Kaboo runs, and why each setting is there.

## The setup

```yaml
attachments:
  default: reference
  tool: true
  base_url: ${API_BASE_URL:-http://localhost:3000}
  authorization: forwarded_props:runToken
  content_url_template: /api/storage/download/{id}

agents:
  orchestrator: {}                       # manifest + fetch tool
  chart_reviewer:
    attachments: {inline: true}          # also sees images directly
  formatter:
    attachments: none                    # never needs the files
```

- **`default: reference`** gives every agent a manifest of what the user
  attached and nothing heavier. A manifest line costs a few tokens; an inlined
  PDF costs thousands on every turn it stays in history.
- **`tool: true`** grants `list_references` and `fetch_attachment`, so an agent
  pulls a file's content only when its task needs it.
- **`base_url` + `authorization`** let the server fetch files from your own API
  with the caller's token, taken from the run's `forwardedProps`. The token is
  sent only to URLs under `base_url`; presigned and third-party URLs are
  fetched without it.
- **`content_url_template`** makes a file fetchable on *every* turn, not only
  the turn it was attached on — the client sends the file's id in state, and
  the template turns it into a URL.
- **`inline: true`** only on the agent that must see pixels, on a model that
  can. Everyone else works from the manifest.

## Tools that return images

A tool behind an MCP gateway can only answer in text, so return images as
base64 inside the result's JSON under `attachments`. The library strips them
out of the text and hands them to the model as image blocks of the same tool
result
([Chapter 19](../configuration/Chapter_19.md#media-a-tool-returns)):

```json
{
  "summary": "3 problems in 2 of 11 widgets",
  "attachments": [{"name": "Rows 1-7", "mime_type": "image/jpeg", "data": "<base64>"}]
}
```

Kaboo uses this to close the loop on dashboards: after building one, the
visualizer calls a verification tool that renders the dashboard in a headless
browser and returns screenshots, and the agent fixes what it can see — a
chart with no data, a title cut off — before it reports back. Agents that can
see their output catch problems no schema check will.

Keep images small and few: at most 8 per result are unpacked, each up to
3.75 MB, and every one stays in the agent's history.

## Custom kinds of reference

Users can cite things that are not files — a table, a dashboard, a ticket.
These arrive as references with a `kind` and an `id`, appear in the same
manifest, and are resolved by your own tools (`get_dashboard(id)`), not by
`fetch_attachment`. A data source cited this way is also what
[tag-activated skills](skills.md#which-skills-an-agent-gets) match on.

## Frontend

kaboo-react mints the reference ids, sends files as multimodal message parts on
the turn they are attached and as state on later turns, and renders the
attachment chips
([Chapter 19](../configuration/Chapter_19.md#frontend-wiring-kaboo-react)).

# docs/recipes/chat-ui-activity.md

# Sub-agents in a chat UI

A multi-agent run can take minutes. Users trust it when they can see it
working — which specialist is on the job, what it is doing right now, in
words rather than function names. Every agent a delegate runs streams on the
wire as AG-UI's own sub-agent events, and kaboo-react folds them into cards.

## What the client receives

The entry agent's stream *is* the chat reply: its text and tool calls arrive as
ordinary AG-UI events. Each agent it delegates to, at any depth, arrives as one
invocation:

- **`SUBAGENT_STARTED`** opens it, with a `subagentRunId`, the agent's `name`,
  the `parentToolCallId` of the delegating call and the
  `parentSubagentRunId` of the invocation that made that call. `metadata`
  holds its `title` and the `task` it was handed.
- **Its text, reasoning and tool calls** follow as the standard events, each
  tagged with its `subagentRunId`. Tool arguments stream as the model writes
  them, so a UI can draw a widget or a query while it is being written.
- **`TOOL_CALL_RESULT`** carries each result. Its `metadata` holds the tool's
  `label`, a `status` of `success` or `error` and, for a failed call, the
  `error` to show and the `fix` when the service suggests one; `approval` when
  the call needed one
  ([Human-in-the-loop](../workflows/human-in-the-loop.md#remembered-approvals)).
  A long JSON result stays valid JSON ([Long tool results](#long-tool-results)).
- **`SUBAGENT_FINISHED`** closes it: `completed` with its `result`, or
  `suspended` while it waits on a question or an approval. `metadata` holds its
  token `usage`, its `cost` and, for a
  [structured output](structured-outputs.md), the `outputSchema` name.
- **`SUBAGENT_ERROR`** closes it when it fails.

Each agent's messages only grow at the end: the entry agent, and each
invocation, extends only the newest message it started. Text continues text, a
tool call joins the text or calls just before it, and anything else starts a new
message. A client that appends events as they arrive therefore draws every agent
in the order it worked, whether its model reasoned before or after it spoke. A
call made after reasoning gets an assistant message of its own instead of
joining the text from before that reasoning.

A paused invocation keeps its `subagentRunId`, so the run that resumes it opens
a new segment of the same card. The events are stored and replayed like any
others, so a reload draws the same cards. `RUN_FINISHED.usage` counts every
agent, so a UI can show a true total.

## Name the cards

```yaml
agents:
  orchestrator:
    model: default
  sql_analyst:
    stream:
      title: Analyzing SQL data
  sql_visualizer:
    stream:
      group: sql_visualization
      title: Creating SQL visualizations
```

Titles are what a user reads, so write them as what the agent is *doing*,
and in the user's language — "Analyzing SQL data", not "sql_analyst". An agent
with no title gets one derived from its name, which is rarely the phrase you
would choose. Agents that share a `group` render as one card, which suits a
pair that works on the same thing in turn.

## Label the tools

```yaml
mcp_clients:
  web_research:
    url: ${GATEWAY_URL}
    transport: streamable-http
    params:
      tool_filters:
        allowed: [web-research___search, web-research___read_pages]
    tool_labels:
      web-research___search: Searching the web
      web-research___read_pages: Reading web pages
```

A sub-agent's tool call carries its label in the `metadata.label` of its
`TOOL_CALL_START` and `TOOL_CALL_RESULT`, and the card shows "Reading web pages"
instead of `web-research___read_pages`. Labels can also be set per agent, under
`agents.<name>.tool_labels`.

## Long tool results

A result longer than 16,000 characters is cut to fit. A JSON result stays valid
JSON: lists are cut to their first items and long strings end in "…", and the
object that held each cut key records in `_truncated` how many items or
characters it lost, so a table can say "+190 more":

```json
{"columns":["id","name"],"untrusted_content":{"rows":[[1,"Acme"],[2,"Globex"]],"_truncated":{"rows":190}}}
```

A cut top-level list arrives as `{"items": [...], "_truncated": {"items": N}}`.
Text that is not JSON is cut and ends in `...`.

## Test it

`TurnResult.groups` holds the cards as a client folds them, so a test can assert
what a user would see — which agents worked, nested under whom, and with which
tools ([Testing](../testing.md#multi-agent-runs)). Lab scenarios:
[delegate-dashboard](https://github.com/gl-pgege/kaboo-docs/blob/main/examples/kaboo-workflows-demo/scenarios/delegate-dashboard.yaml),
[nested-dashboard](https://github.com/gl-pgege/kaboo-docs/blob/main/examples/kaboo-workflows-demo/scenarios/nested-dashboard.yaml)
and
[parallel-dashboard](https://github.com/gl-pgege/kaboo-docs/blob/main/examples/kaboo-workflows-demo/scenarios/parallel-dashboard.yaml).

# docs/recipes/cost-and-context.md

# Cost and context control

A data-analysis run can make dozens of model calls, each resending a long
system prompt, a tool list and every earlier tool result. Most of the cost —
and most context-window trouble — comes from that resending. Each setting
below is documented in its chapter; this recipe is the combination Kaboo runs,
in order of payoff.

## 1. Cache what every call repeats

```yaml
models:
  default:
    provider: bedrock
    model_id: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5
    params:
      cache_config:
        strategy: auto             # the conversation up to the last message
        system_prompt_ttl: true    # the system prompt
        tools_ttl: true            # the tool list
      max_tokens: 32000
```

Three of Bedrock's four cache points: a tool loop re-reads its system prompt,
tools and earlier turns from the cache instead of paying for them again on
every call. Loaded history keeps a cache point of its own
([Multi-turn history](../workflows/multi-turn-history.md#loaded-memory-is-cached-on-bedrock)).
Anything that rewrites the start of the prompt on every call — a timestamp at
the top of a system prompt, say — defeats the cache; append such lines at the
end instead.

## 2. Think where it pays

```yaml
models:
  default:
    thinking: {effort: high, display: summarized}

agents:
  orchestrator:
    thinking: {effort: medium}     # routing and synthesis
  sql_analyst:
    thinking: false                # writes code against a known schema
```

Set thinking on the model as a default, then turn it down per agent
([Chapter 2](../configuration/Chapter_02.md#thinking)). Agents doing
mechanical work against clear instructions rarely gain from it; the agent that
plans and judges does. Adaptive thinking needs a model that supports it — a
config written for Sonnet 5 sent to an older model fails at the provider.

## 3. Clear old tool results

```yaml
agents:
  sql_analyst:
    context:
      clear_tool_results:
        trigger: 60000
        keep_last: 3
        keep_tools: [sql___get_schema]
```

Query results are the bulk of a long analysis, and an agent rarely needs the
ninth-from-last one verbatim. Past the trigger, older results are replaced by a
line naming the tool and the ids in the result, so the agent can fetch again
what it actually needs ([Chapter 8](../configuration/Chapter_08.md#clearing-old-tool-results)).
Keep reference results such as a schema.

## 4. Bound what carries across turns

```yaml
agents:
  orchestrator:
    conversation_manager:
      type: strands.agent:SlidingWindowConversationManager
      params: {window_size: 80}
    history:
      group: orchestrator
  sql_analyst:
    history:
      group: sql
      keep: masked
      summarize_over: 40000
      summarize_model: utility
```

A sliding window bounds what an agent keeps within a run. History bounds what
it carries into the next turn: masked history writes back each finished tool
result as a one-line pointer the agent can call again, and `summarize_over`
has a cheap model condense the oldest calls once the masked memory still grows
too large
([Multi-turn history](../workflows/multi-turn-history.md#keeping-a-masked-memory)).
Agents that share a history `group` share one memory — useful when two agents
take turns as the same voice.

## 5. Keep toolboxes small

Every tool's schema rides along on every call, and a model choosing among
forty tools chooses worse than one choosing among eight. Kaboo refuses a
workflow that gives an agent more than 20 tools, and splits each service's
tools into narrow MCP clients — an `_explore` client for read-only discovery
beside the full one — so an agent is granted exactly what its job needs
([Call MCP tools as the signed-in user](user-identity-mcp.md#relay-the-token-on-every-mcp-call)).

## 6. Put ceilings on runaway work

- `MaxToolCallsGuard` caps tool calls per invocation, so a confused agent stops
  instead of looping ([Chapter 6](../configuration/Chapter_06.md)).
- [Refusing repeated failures](guard-hooks.md#refuse-a-call-that-has-already-failed-twice)
  stops the commonest loop of all: the same broken call, again.
- A small, deterministic model for utility work — naming a conversation,
  classifying a request — costs a fraction of the analyst model:

    ```yaml
    models:
      utility:
        provider: bedrock
        model_id: us.anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5-20251001-v1:0
        params: {temperature: 0, max_tokens: 200}
    ```

## Measure it

Token usage per run arrives in the activity stream and in `TurnResult.usage_by_run`
in tests; with [telemetry](../evaluation.md#enable-telemetry) on, every model
call's tokens and latency land in your tracing backend. Measure before and
after each change — caching in particular is easy to break silently.

# docs/recipes/generative-ui.md

# Generative UI from any agent

CopilotKit draws UI from what an agent streams, at four levels of freedom:
your own components for your own tools, declarative surfaces from a catalog
(A2UI), one-off sandboxed visuals (Open Generative UI), and apps an MCP server
ships (MCP Apps). The first three run in CopilotKit's runtime as middleware over
the agent's stream; kaboo-workflows' part is to put every agent's tool calls on
the wire, delegates included, and to give each agent only the tiers it may use.

## Your components for your tools

Every agent's tool calls stream with their arguments as the model writes them,
sub-agents' tagged with their `subagentRunId`. A client renderer keyed by tool
name (CopilotKit's `renderToolCalls`, or a kaboo-react card) draws a widget, a
query or a dashboard while it is being written, in the chat or inside the
sub-agent's card alike. Nothing to configure here.

## Declarative surfaces (A2UI)

```yaml
agents:
  analyst:
    client_tools: [render_a2ui]
```

- **`render_a2ui` is offered to the agents allowed it.** The client sends its
  catalog as context; kaboo-workflows gives each allowed agent a `render_a2ui`
  tool described by that catalog, and the catalog reaches no other agent.
- **The surface paints from the streamed arguments.** CopilotKit's A2UI
  middleware draws it in the chat as the call streams, from a delegate as from
  the entry agent.
- **The tool doesn't wait.** It checks the components against the catalog and
  answers "Rendered surface …", or names what is wrong so the model fixes it
  and calls again.
- **An action on a surface is the person's turn.** A button that isn't handled
  in the browser reaches the agent as `forwardedProps.a2uiAction`, and the
  agent reads it as a message: `I used "break_down" on the "churn" surface (by: segment).`

Widgets in a catalog should take an id (a saved query's) rather than data, so a
surface stays small and its numbers stay live.

## One-off visuals (Open Generative UI)

```yaml
agents:
  analyst:
    client_tools: [generateSandboxedUi]
```

`generateSandboxedUi` is a browser tool: CopilotKit's Open Generative UI
middleware renders its HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a sandboxed iframe as the
arguments stream, and the browser answers the call once it has drawn it. Give
the sandbox read-only functions that fetch data by id (the lab's
`getQueryData`), so the visual carries no data of its own.

## Apps from MCP servers (MCP Apps)

A tool whose MCP server ships a UI resource reaches the run through
CopilotKit's MCP Apps middleware, which adds the server's model-visible tools
to `RunAgentInput.tools` under their own names. Allow them like any browser
tool:

```yaml
agents:
  analyst:
    client_tools: [partner_benchmarks]
```

The call waits like a browser tool. The middleware runs it against its server
when the run ends waiting on it, sends its result and the app to the chat, and
kaboo-runtime goes on with the agent in the same run, so the turn finishes with
the agent's answer. Tools the server marks as visible to the app only never
reach a model.

## Which one to use

Use your own components, or A2UI, for anything that is yours to design; Open
Generative UI for a visual no component covers; and MCP Apps for UI that comes
from a server you don't own. Say where an answer goes in the agent's prompt,
for example:

```text
Where an answer goes:
- A short fact: one or two sentences.
- A figure, a trend or a small table that answers the question now: render it
  inline with render_a2ui.
- Several parts, or anything worth keeping: a dashboard on the canvas.
- A one-off visual no catalog component covers: generateSandboxedUi.
```

Lab scenarios:
[a2ui-inline](https://github.com/gl-pgege/kaboo-docs/blob/main/examples/kaboo-workflows-demo/scenarios/a2ui-inline.yaml),
[a2ui-subagent](https://github.com/gl-pgege/kaboo-docs/blob/main/examples/kaboo-workflows-demo/scenarios/a2ui-subagent.yaml),
[a2ui-action](https://github.com/gl-pgege/kaboo-docs/blob/main/examples/kaboo-workflows-demo/scenarios/a2ui-action.yaml),
[ogui-visual](https://github.com/gl-pgege/kaboo-docs/blob/main/examples/kaboo-workflows-demo/scenarios/ogui-visual.yaml),
[mcp-partner](https://github.com/gl-pgege/kaboo-docs/blob/main/examples/kaboo-workflows-demo/scenarios/mcp-partner.yaml)
and
[viewer-parity](https://github.com/gl-pgege/kaboo-docs/blob/main/examples/kaboo-workflows-demo/scenarios/viewer-parity.yaml).

# docs/recipes/guard-hooks.md

# Guard hooks for every agent

Some failures have nothing to do with any particular workflow: a transcript
the provider rejects, a model retrying the same broken call, a user whose
sign-in expires mid-run. Hooks
([Chapter 6](../configuration/Chapter_06.md)) are where to catch them, once,
for every agent. These are the guards Kaboo puts on every agent of every
workflow.

## Answer every tool call before the model sees the transcript

Bedrock rejects a turn unless every tool call in an assistant message is
answered by a tool result in the very next message — and strands reacts to the
rejection by stopping the run silently. Transcripts break this rule more often
than you would think: a turn cut off mid-tools, an interrupted call replayed
from the client, a message the host persisted twice. Bedrock is just as strict
about two messages in a row from the same role, and about empty text blocks.

Repairing the transcript before every model call turns each of those into a
run that carries on:

```python
from typing import Any

from strands.hooks import HookProvider, HookRegistry
from strands.hooks.events import BeforeModelCallEvent

UNANSWERED = (
    "This call did not run: the turn that made it ended before it could. "
    "Call it again if you still need its result."
)


def _blank(block: Any) -> bool:
    return isinstance(block, dict) and set(block) == {"text"} and not str(block["text"]).strip()


def alternating(messages: list[dict]) -> list[dict]:
    merged: list[dict] = []
    for message in messages:
        content = [b for b in message.get("content") or [] if not _blank(b)]
        if not content:
            continue
        if merged and merged[-1]["role"] == message["role"]:
            merged[-1] = {**merged[-1], "content": merged[-1]["content"] + content}
        else:
            merged.append({**message, "content": content})
    for message in merged:
        if message["role"] == "user":
            results = [b for b in message["content"] if "toolResult" in b]
            message["content"] = results + [b for b in message["content"] if b not in results]
    return merged


def answered(messages: list[dict]) -> list[dict]:
    messages = alternating(messages)
    repaired: list[dict] = []
    for index, message in enumerate(messages):
        repaired.append(message)
        if message["role"] != "assistant":
            continue
        asked = [b["toolUse"]["toolUseId"] for b in message["content"] if "toolUse" in b]
        following = messages[index + 1] if index + 1 < len(messages) else None
        replies = following if following and following["role"] == "user" else None
        given = {
            b["toolResult"]["toolUseId"]
            for b in (replies or {}).get("content", [])
            if "toolResult" in b
        }
        missing = [
            {"toolResult": {"toolUseId": t, "status": "error", "content": [{"text": UNANSWERED}]}}
            for t in asked
            if t not in given
        ]
        if not missing:
            continue
        if replies is not None:
            replies["content"] = missing + replies["content"]
        else:
            repaired.append({"role": "user", "content": missing})
    return repaired


class AnswerEveryToolUse(HookProvider):
    def register_hooks(self, registry: HookRegistry, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        registry.add_callback(BeforeModelCallEvent, self._answer)

    def _answer(self, event: BeforeModelCallEvent) -> None:
        event.agent.messages[:] = answered(event.agent.messages)


broken = [
    {"role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Run the report"}]},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": [{"toolUse": {"toolUseId": "t1", "name": "run", "input": {}}}]},
    {"role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Any news?"}]},
]
fixed = answered(broken)
assert fixed[2]["content"][0]["toolResult"]["toolUseId"] == "t1"
```

The inserted result is an error the model can read, so it calls the tool again
if it still needs it.

## Refuse a call that has already failed twice

A model that gets an error back sometimes sends the identical call again, and
again. Refusing the third identical attempt, with a message telling it to
change course, breaks the loop without ending the run:

```python
import json
from typing import Any

from strands.hooks import HookProvider, HookRegistry
from strands.hooks.events import AfterToolCallEvent, BeforeInvocationEvent, BeforeToolCallEvent

REPEATED_FAILURE = (
    "This exact call has already failed twice, so it was not sent again. Read the "
    "earlier errors, then change the arguments or take a different approach."
)


def failed(result: Any) -> bool:
    return isinstance(result, dict) and result.get("status") == "error"


class RefuseRepeatedFailures(HookProvider):
    def __init__(self, limit: int = 2) -> None:
        self.limit = limit
        self.failures: dict[str, int] = {}

    def register_hooks(self, registry: HookRegistry, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        registry.add_callback(BeforeInvocationEvent, lambda event: self.failures.clear())
        registry.add_callback(BeforeToolCallEvent, self._refuse)
        registry.add_callback(AfterToolCallEvent, self._count)

    @staticmethod
    def _key(tool_use: Any) -> str:
        return json.dumps([tool_use.get("name"), tool_use.get("input")], sort_keys=True, default=str)

    def _refuse(self, event: BeforeToolCallEvent) -> None:
        if self.failures.get(self._key(event.tool_use), 0) >= self.limit:
            event.cancel_tool = REPEATED_FAILURE

    def _count(self, event: AfterToolCallEvent) -> None:
        key = self._key(event.tool_use)
        if failed(event.result):
            self.failures[key] = self.failures.get(key, 0) + 1
        else:
            self.failures.pop(key, None)
```

The key is the tool name *and* its input: the same tool with different
arguments is a new attempt, which is exactly what the message asks for. Ours
also counts a result whose JSON body says `"success": false` or carries an
`"error"`, since many MCP services report failure that way. The library's
`MaxToolCallsGuard` is the coarser companion: a ceiling on tool calls per
invocation, whatever they are.

## Stop when the sign-in expires

A run relaying the user's token ([Call MCP tools as the signed-in
user](user-identity-mcp.md)) can outlive it, and then every tool call fails
authorization. Check the token's expiry before each model call and each tool
call, and answer with one clear message instead:

```python
import time
from typing import Any

from strands.hooks import HookProvider, HookRegistry
from strands.hooks.events import BeforeModelCallEvent, BeforeToolCallEvent
from strands.models import Model

from kaboo_workflows import get_auth_context

SIGNED_OUT = (
    "Your sign-in expired while I was working, so I stopped here. Sign in again "
    "and send your question once more; what I built so far is kept."
)


def signed_out() -> bool:
    principal = get_auth_context()
    expiry = principal.claims.get("exp") if principal else None
    return isinstance(expiry, (int, float)) and time.time() >= expiry


class SignedOutModel(Model):
    def update_config(self, **model_config: Any) -> None:
        pass

    def get_config(self) -> Any:
        return {}

    def structured_output(self, *args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> Any:
        raise NotImplementedError

    async def stream(self, *args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> Any:
        yield {"messageStart": {"role": "assistant"}}
        yield {"contentBlockDelta": {"delta": {"text": SIGNED_OUT}}}
        yield {"contentBlockStop": {}}
        yield {"messageStop": {"stopReason": "end_turn"}}


class StopOnExpiredSignIn(HookProvider):
    def register_hooks(self, registry: HookRegistry, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        registry.add_callback(BeforeModelCallEvent, self._answer_signed_out)
        registry.add_callback(BeforeToolCallEvent, self._refuse_tool)

    def _answer_signed_out(self, event: BeforeModelCallEvent) -> None:
        if signed_out():
            event.agent.model = SignedOutModel()

    def _refuse_tool(self, event: BeforeToolCallEvent) -> None:
        if signed_out():
            event.cancel_tool = SIGNED_OUT


assert not signed_out()
```

Swapping in a model that replies with the message makes it the agent's answer,
so it reaches the chat like any other reply. An agent with an `output_schema`
cannot answer in prose; on strands versions with `AfterToolsEvent`, ours
cancels such an agent's invocation and ends its turn after the current tools
instead.

## Two small ones

- **Today's date.** Models do not know what day it is. A
  `BeforeInvocationEvent` hook that appends "Today's date is …" in the user's
  time zone (`get_forwarded_props()["timezone"]`) to the system prompt fixes
  every "last month" question.
- **Model timing.** A `BeforeModelCallEvent` / `AfterModelCallEvent` pair that
  logs each call's latency, time to first event and retry count with the run id
  (`get_run_id()`) answers "why was that slow?" without a tracing backend.

## Put them on every agent

Either add them when composing the workflow, as Kaboo does
([Compose a workflow per run](per-run-workflows.md)), or declare them once in
the config and alias them:

```yaml
x-guards: &guards
  - my_service.hooks:AnswerEveryToolUse
  - my_service.hooks:RefuseRepeatedFailures
  - my_service.hooks:StopOnExpiredSignIn

agents:
  analyst:
    hooks: *guards
  visualizer:
    hooks: *guards
```

`x-` blocks exist only to hold anchors; the loader strips them
([Chapter 4](../configuration/Chapter_04.md)).

## Test them

Each guard has a failure it exists for, so script the model into that failure
and assert the run survived it — a broken transcript passed in as `messages`,
the same failing call scripted three times
([Testing](../testing.md#hooks-and-guards)).

# docs/recipes/index.md

# Recipes

The configuration chapters say what every field does. These recipes show how
the pieces fit together in a real service — each one is a pattern running in
production in [Kaboo](https://gl-pgege.github.io/kaboo-docs/), written so you
can lift it into your own project.

| Recipe | Reach for it when |
|--------|-------------------|
| [Serve on AgentCore in production](production-serving.md) | You deploy behind AWS AgentCore Runtime, or any host with response caps and idle reaping |
| [Compose a workflow per run](per-run-workflows.md) | One service runs many workflows — per tenant, per project, per admin-authored row |
| [Skills](skills.md) | Agents need reusable instructions, loaded only when a task calls for them |
| [Call MCP tools as the signed-in user](user-identity-mcp.md) | Tools behind a gateway must act with the caller's permissions |
| [Tools that need run context](tools-with-run-context.md) | A tool keeps state per conversation or must act once per turn |
| [Guard hooks for every agent](guard-hooks.md) | Runs should survive malformed transcripts, retry loops and expired sign-ins |
| [Ask the user, and request inputs](asking-the-user.md) | An agent needs an answer, a file or a data source mid-run |
| [Shared state](shared-state.md) | The person and every agent should see what the conversation built, without looking it up |
| [Generative UI from any agent](generative-ui.md) | Answers should come as surfaces, visuals or partner apps in the chat |
| [Structured outputs a UI can render](structured-outputs.md) | An agent's result should arrive as typed data for a card, not prose |
| [Images and file attachments](attachments-and-images.md) | Users attach files, or tools return images |
| [Sub-agents in a chat UI](chat-ui-activity.md) | Users should see which agent is working on what, in words |
| [Cost and context control](cost-and-context.md) | Long, tool-heavy runs cost too much or outgrow the context window |

[Testing your workflows](../testing.md) covers proving any of these with a
scripted model, and [Best practices](../best-practices.md) collects the rules
of thumb behind them.

# docs/recipes/per-run-workflows.md

# Compose a workflow per run

One service can run a different workflow on every request: a workflow per
tenant, per project, per row an admin edits in a UI. Nothing is restarted and
nothing is read from disk at run time. The host stores workflows, composes the
final YAML for each run, and submits it with the run; the agent service layers
it over its own base config
([Chapter 17](../configuration/Chapter_17.md#when-the-config-itself-is-per-request),
`examples/21_runtime_configs/`).

## Split the config in two

**The base config** lives with the service and holds what every workflow
shares, including anything secret:

```yaml
# config.yaml — the service's own file
models:
  analyst-model:
    provider: bedrock
    model_id: ${BEDROCK_MODEL_ID:-us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5}
    params: {region_name: "${BEDROCK_REGION:-us-east-1}"}

mcp_clients:
  sql:
    url: ${GATEWAY_URL}
    transport: streamable-http
    auth: {type: relay}
    params:
      tool_filters: {allowed: [sql___run_query, sql___get_schema]}

attachments:
  default: reference

agents:
  assistant:                       # the fallback when a run submits nothing
    model: analyst-model
    system_prompt: You are a helpful data assistant.
entry: assistant
```

**A stored workflow** holds only `agents`, `orchestrations` and `entry`, and
refers to models and MCP clients by name:

```yaml
agents:
  analyst:
    model: analyst-model
    mcp: [sql]
    system_prompt: You answer questions from the sales database.
entry: analyst
```

The overlay replaces the base's `agents`, `orchestrations` and `entry`, adds to
its `models` and `mcp_clients`, and may not declare `mcp_servers` at all — a run
may not launch a process. Stored workflows that only *name* the base's models
and clients never carry a URL or a credential.

## Compose, then submit

Composition is plain dictionary work on the host. Ours applies the user's
choices (thinking level, model override), drops agents for data sources the run
does not have, inlines [skills](skills.md), adds the
[hooks every agent needs](guard-hooks.md), stamps today's date, and fills in
IDs such as the current project:

```python
import yaml

from kaboo_workflows import load_session_config, parse_config_sources

EVERY_AGENT_HOOKS = ["my_service.hooks:AnswerEveryToolUse"]


def compose(stored: str, *, project_id: str) -> str:
    doc = yaml.safe_load(stored)
    for agent in doc.get("agents", {}).values():
        agent["hooks"] = [*agent.get("hooks", []), *EVERY_AGENT_HOOKS]
    text = yaml.safe_dump(doc, sort_keys=False)
    text = text.replace("{{project_id}}", project_id)
    return text.replace("${", "$${")


STORED = """
agents:
  analyst:
    model: analyst-model
    system_prompt: |
      You answer questions about project {{project_id}}.
      Quote templates such as ${name} literally.
entry: analyst
"""

BASE = parse_config_sources("""
models:
  analyst-model: {provider: bedrock, model_id: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5}
agents:
  assistant: {model: analyst-model, system_prompt: Fallback.}
entry: assistant
""")

composed = compose(STORED, project_id="p-42")
config = load_session_config(BASE, composed)

prompt = config.agents["analyst"].system_prompt
assert "project p-42" in prompt
assert "${name}" in prompt
assert config.agents["analyst"].hooks == EVERY_AGENT_HOOKS
```

The run then carries the composed text in `forwardedProps`, under the key the
service was started with (`create_agui_app(session_config_key="workflow_config")`):

```json
{
  "threadId": "t-1",
  "runId": "r-1",
  "messages": [{"id": "m-1", "role": "user", "content": "How did Q3 go?"}],
  "forwardedProps": {"workflow_config": "agents:\n  analyst: ..."}
}
```

## Escape interpolation in anything authored outside the repository

A submitted workflow is interpolated against **the service's environment**, on
purpose, so an admin-authored config can say `${API_KEY}` without the secret
living in the database. The flip side: any `${…}` in user-authored text — a
prompt that quotes template syntax, or one written to fish for
`${AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY}` — resolves against the server too.

`$${` is the escape for a literal `${`. We escape every `${` in the composed
workflow, which means stored workflows never read the environment and
everything secret stays in the base config. If your workflow authors are
trusted and need environment values, escape only the fields they write freely,
such as prompts.

## Keep it safe and testable

- **Validate on save**, with the same loader a run uses
  ([production recipe](production-serving.md#validate-a-workflow-before-saving-it)),
  so a broken workflow is an error in the editor rather than a failed run.
- **Pass `allowed_mcp_hosts`** to `create_agui_app` and `load_session_config`
  if a workflow can declare its own MCP clients.
- **Refuse leftovers.** After filling placeholders, fail composition if any
  remain; a prompt that still says `{{dashboard_id}}` produces confident
  nonsense.
- **Test the composed text**, not the stored one:
  `Pipeline(base, session_config_key="workflow_config")` with the composer's
  output in `forwarded_props` runs it end to end
  ([Testing](../testing.md#runtime-composed-workflows)).

# docs/recipes/production-serving.md

# Serve on AgentCore in production

`create_agui_app` already speaks AgentCore Runtime's HTTP contract: AG-UI on
`POST /invocations`, a health check on `GET /ping`. This recipe covers what a
production deployment adds on top — the settings worth turning on, and four
behaviours of the host that the defaults do not account for.

## The app

```{.python notest}
import os
from pathlib import Path

import strands.models.bedrock as bedrock

from kaboo_workflows.adapters import create_agui_app

from my_service.auth import verify_run_token

bedrock.DEFAULT_READ_TIMEOUT = int(os.environ.get("BEDROCK_READ_TIMEOUT", "300"))

app = create_agui_app(
    Path(__file__).parent / "config.yaml",
    session_config_key="workflow_config",
    allowed_mcp_hosts=["gateway.internal.example.com"],
    auth=verify_run_token,
    ping_path=None,
)
```

- **`session_config_key`** lets each run bring its own workflow, layered over
  the base config — see [Compose a workflow per run](per-run-workflows.md).
  Without it, the service serves its own config, and each conversation gets its
  own agents the first time it runs (the 256 most recent are kept), so one
  person's sub-agent paused on a question never turns up in another's chat.
- **`allowed_mcp_hosts`** bounds what a submitted workflow's MCP clients may
  connect to. Set it whenever workflows are authored anywhere but your
  repository: an arbitrary URL needs no code to exfiltrate data.
- **`auth`** verifies every request and binds the caller, so MCP tools can run
  as them — see [Call MCP tools as the signed-in user](user-identity-mcp.md).
- **`ping_path=None`** because the packaged health check always answers
  healthy, and AgentCore needs more than that (below).
- **The Bedrock read timeout** defaults to strands' value, which a long
  thinking turn can exceed. Raise it for the slowest call you expect.

AgentCore Runtime expects the container on port 8080.

## Report busy while a run is open

AgentCore decides a session is idle from its `/ping` status, not from whether a
request is still on the wire. A session that only ever answers `Healthy` can be
reaped mid-run, which reaches the user as a stream that ends with no terminal
event. Answer `HealthyBusy` while any invocation is open:

```{.python notest}
class RunCounter:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.active = 0

    @property
    def status(self) -> str:
        return "HealthyBusy" if self.active else "Healthy"


runs = RunCounter()


@app.get("/ping")
def ping() -> dict[str, str]:
    return {"status": runs.status}
```

Increment `runs.active` when a `POST /invocations` arrives and decrement it when
the response ends — in the ASGI middleware below, which sees both.

## Stay under the response cap

AgentCore closes the socket once a response reaches 100 MiB, with no error of
its own. The run dies without a terminal event, and CopilotKit reports
whichever tool call was open as failed — the user is told a healthy tool broke.

A response carries only what its turn adds, never the conversation again (see
[Response size](../concepts.md#response-size)), so a turn would need tens of
megabytes of new tool results to come near the cap. Keep a backstop anyway:
wrap the ASGI `send` so it forwards whole SSE frames, and once the budget is
spent, close the stream with a real `RUN_FINISHED` and a short message saying
the answer was cut off. A truncated answer with a reason beats a failure with
none.

```{.python notest}
AGENTCORE_RESPONSE_CAP = 104_857_600
HARD_BUDGET = AGENTCORE_RESPONSE_CAP - 10 * 1024 * 1024
```

The margin under the cap leaves room for the closing events and for
chunked-transfer framing, which counts against the cap but is not yours to
measure. When cutting the stream, split only on the blank line between SSE
frames — cutting an arbitrary chunk leaves the client half an event.

## Non-streaming calls over `/invocations`

AgentCore Runtime forwards only `POST /invocations`. Anything else your service
answers — validating a workflow before an admin saves it, running a workflow
once for a background job — has to ride that path too. Dispatch on a field in
the body, in a **pure ASGI** middleware, and replay the body downstream for
ordinary AG-UI runs:

```{.python notest}
class NonStreamingOverInvocations:
    def __init__(self, app, runs: RunCounter) -> None:
        self.app = app
        self.runs = runs

    async def __call__(self, scope, receive, send) -> None:
        if scope["type"] != "http" or scope["path"] != "/invocations" or scope["method"] != "POST":
            await self.app(scope, receive, send)
            return
        self.runs.active += 1
        try:
            body = await read_body(receive)
            if b'"my_validate"' in body[:4096]:
                await answer_validation(body, scope, send)
                return
            await self.app(scope, replay(body, receive), budgeted(send, body))
        finally:
            self.runs.active -= 1


app.add_middleware(NonStreamingOverInvocations, runs=runs)
```

Starlette's `BaseHTTPMiddleware` will not do here: once it has consumed the
body, its disconnect listener receives the replayed `http.request` and breaks
the downstream SSE stream. Authenticate the non-streaming branches with the
same verifier the AG-UI path uses.

## Validate a workflow before saving it

`load_session_config` runs the same overlay, schema and reference checks a run
would, without building anything:

```{.python notest}
from kaboo_workflows import load_session_config, parse_config_sources

BASE_RAW = parse_config_sources("config.yaml")


def validate(workflow_yaml: str) -> dict:
    try:
        config = load_session_config(
            BASE_RAW, workflow_yaml, allowed_mcp_hosts=["gateway.internal.example.com"]
        )
    except Exception as exc:
        return {"valid": False, "error": str(exc)}
    return {"valid": True, "entry": config.entry, "agents": sorted(config.agents)}
```

The error names the bad reference and lists what is available, which makes it
a good message to show an admin. Add your own rules after it. Ours refuse an
agent holding more than 20 tools, a tool granted twice by overlapping MCP
clients, and a prompt that names a tool the agent is not granted.

## Run a workflow once, without streaming

For a background job, build the run the same way a streamed run is built and
answer with the final text:

```{.python notest}
from dataclasses import replace

from kaboo_workflows import (
    load_session,
    load_session_config,
    resolve_infra,
    resolve_run_clients,
    set_auth_context,
    validate_raw_config,
)

BASE_INFRA = resolve_infra(validate_raw_config(BASE_RAW))


async def run_once(workflow_yaml: str, prompt: str, principal) -> str:
    config = load_session_config(BASE_RAW, workflow_yaml, allowed_mcp_hosts=ALLOWED)
    set_auth_context(principal)
    clients = resolve_run_clients(config, BASE_INFRA)
    clients.start(pin_clients=False)
    try:
        resolved = load_session(
            config, replace(BASE_INFRA, clients=clients.clients, mcp_lifecycle=clients)
        )
        result = await resolved.entry.invoke_async(prompt)
        return str(result).strip()
    finally:
        clients.stop()
```

`set_auth_context` comes first so relayed MCP calls go out as the caller, and
the run's clients stop with the call, as they do with a streamed run.

## Related

- [Chapter 17: when the config itself is per-request](../configuration/Chapter_17.md#when-the-config-itself-is-per-request)
- [Evaluation: enable telemetry](../evaluation.md#enable-telemetry) for traces
  in Langfuse or any OTLP backend
- `examples/agentcore/` for inbound auth styles on AgentCore

# docs/recipes/shared-state.md

# Shared state: state effects and workspace views

A conversation builds things — dashboards, saved queries, a report — and the
person and every agent need to know what exists without asking for it. Two
pieces of config keep that in the AG-UI state the conversation already carries:

- **State effects** write a tool's result into the state the moment the call
  succeeds. The client receives each change as a `STATE_DELTA`, so a canvas can
  follow the agent while it works.
- **Workspace views** show an agent parts of that state at every model call, so
  it extends what was built instead of listing and reading it first.

## Write what a tool did

```yaml
state_effects:
  - tool: sql-workbench___create_queries
    mapper: my_service.effects:queries_saved
  - tool: "dashboard___*_widgets"          # an fnmatch glob
    mapper: my_service.effects:dashboard_changed
  - tool: project___get_context
    path: /kaboo_workspace/project          # the parsed result, written whole
```

An effect names a tool, or a glob of names, and either a `path` to write the
tool's parsed result to, or a `mapper`. A mapper receives a
`StateEffectCall` — the tool, its input, its result (the tool's MCP
`structuredContent` when it sends one, otherwise its text, parsed as JSON when it
is JSON), the agent, the run and the state before the effect — and returns JSON
Patch operations. A tool can therefore answer the model in prose and the mapper
in structured data:

```python
from typing import Any

from kaboo_workflows.hooks import StateEffectCall

ROOT = "/kaboo_workspace"


def queries_saved(call: StateEffectCall) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    operations: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
    if "kaboo_workspace" not in call.state:
        operations.append({"op": "add", "path": ROOT, "value": {"queries": {}, "changes": []}})
    for query in (call.result or {}).get("created", []):
        operations.append(
            {"op": "add", "path": f"{ROOT}/queries/{query['query_id']}", "value": {"title": query["title"]}}
        )
    operations.append(
        {"op": "add", "path": f"{ROOT}/changes/-", "value": {"agent": call.agent, "summary": "Saved queries"}}
    )
    return operations
```

- **Effects run for every agent**, delegates included, after a call succeeds. A
  failed call writes nothing.
- **Keep state small and by reference.** Write ids, titles and what changed,
  never data rows: the state travels with every run, and widgets fetch their
  own rows by id.
- **One writer per key.** The agent's effects own `kaboo_workspace`; the
  person's own edits go to the services, and the agent sees them through
  context or the next effect. kaboo-runtime keeps server-owned keys away from
  the browser ([state ownership](https://gl-pgege.github.io/kaboo-runtime/replay-and-state/)).

## Show it to an agent

```yaml
agents:
  analyst:
    workspace: [/kaboo_workspace]
  visualizer:
    workspace: [/kaboo_workspace/dashboards]
```

`workspace` lists JSON Pointers into the state. Before every model call, delegates
included, the agent's latest message opens with what they point at, current as
of that call:

```text
The workspace — what this conversation has built, current as of now:
/kaboo_workspace: {"dashboards":{"d_2":{"title":"Churn by region","version":3}},...}
```

The agent's own conversation is untouched; only what reaches its model changes.
Point each agent at what it needs: a visualizer needs the dashboards, not every
saved query.

## Show what a service holds: working views

The workspace holds what the conversation noted. When the thing itself lives in a
service — the dashboards an agent is building, with every widget and who changed
what — a working view asks the service:

```yaml
agents:
  analyst:
    views: [my_service.views:dashboards]
```

A view is a callable that takes a `ViewRequest` (the agent, the thread and run
ids, whether this is the invocation's first model call, the run's AG-UI context
and the shared state as of the call) and returns a `View` or `None`:

```python
from kaboo_workflows.hooks import View, ViewRequest


def dashboards(request: ViewRequest) -> View | None:
    if request.first_call:
        return View(base=render_dashboards(request.thread_id))
    return View(changes=changes_since_base(request.thread_id, request.agent))
```

- **The base** is kept from the invocation's first model call and opens the
  latest human message with the run's context, so it stays put for the whole
  invocation and a prompt cache over the conversation keeps applying.
- **The changes** are rendered at every model call and end the latest message,
  after the tool results it follows: what the person or other agents changed
  since the base, so the agent keeps their edits without reading the service
  again.
- A view that raises is left out of that call and logged; the run goes on.

A view can also render the state the effects keep. `request.state` is the shared
state as of the call, effects included, so the agent sees its own last write and
what parallel agents built. Text written for a model is shorter and easier to
read than the raw JSON `workspace` pastes:

```python
from kaboo_workflows.hooks import View, ViewRequest


def workspace(request: ViewRequest) -> View | None:
    dashboards = request.state.get("kaboo_workspace", {}).get("dashboards", {})
    if not dashboards:
        return None
    lines = [f'{handle} "{entry["title"]}" v{entry.get("version", 1)}' for handle, entry in dashboards.items()]
    return View(changes="Dashboards in this conversation:\n" + "\n".join(lines))
```

## What it saves

In the lab, extending a dashboard the conversation built takes the agent two
tool calls with a workspace view and four without, the extra two being lookups
(`dashboard___list_dashboards`, `dashboard___get_dashboard`) that only re-read
what the state already held. Run both sides with
`yarn lab compare workspace-vs-read --live` for a real model's numbers.

## Test it

`TurnResult.state()` applies every `STATE_DELTA` the run sent, so a test can
assert what the workspace holds after a turn. Lab scenarios:
[workspace-extend](https://github.com/gl-pgege/kaboo-docs/blob/main/examples/kaboo-workflows-demo/scenarios/workspace-extend.yaml),
[workspace-extend-read](https://github.com/gl-pgege/kaboo-docs/blob/main/examples/kaboo-workflows-demo/scenarios/workspace-extend-read.yaml),
[workspace-refresh](https://github.com/gl-pgege/kaboo-docs/blob/main/examples/kaboo-workflows-demo/scenarios/workspace-refresh.yaml)
and
[delegate-dashboard](https://github.com/gl-pgege/kaboo-docs/blob/main/examples/kaboo-workflows-demo/scenarios/delegate-dashboard.yaml).

# docs/recipes/skills.md

# Skills

A skill is a named piece of instructions — how to write SQL against this
warehouse, how to lay out a dashboard, how to brief a banker on a customer —
that agents use only when a task calls for it. Skills keep system prompts short
and let one well-written instruction serve every agent that needs it.

kaboo-workflows has no `skills:` field of its own. Skills are composed into the
workflow on the host, before the run is submitted — an application of
[Compose a workflow per run](per-run-workflows.md). This recipe is the pattern
Kaboo runs: a skill catalogue in a database, three ways to load a skill, and a
single tool agents call to load one.

## Three loading strategies

| Strategy | What happens | Use it for |
|----------|--------------|------------|
| `full` | Inlined into the agent's system prompt as top-priority rules | Short rules that must always apply: investigation discipline, house style |
| `catalog` | Listed by name and when-to-use; the agent loads it with a tool call | Guides only some tasks need: a tool manual, a web research protocol |
| `rag` | Listed like a catalog skill; the agent loads matching sections by query | Long references: an SDK manual, a widget reference |

Every agent's prompt ends with the skills it has *not* loaded, so an agent can
always discover the one that fits — and most skills cost nothing until used.

## Which skills an agent gets

- **Bound** in the stored workflow, with a host-side key the composer removes
  before submitting:

    ```yaml
    agents:
      sql_analyst:
        skills: [sql-guide, efficiency-discipline]
        mcp: [sql, skills]
    ```

- **Activated by tags.** A skill tagged with a data source's name or kind is
  loaded whenever the run has that data source attached — a skill tagged
  `offers-redshift` switches on for every run that attaches the connection
  named `offers-redshift`. We scope tag-activated skills to the agents that
  work with that kind of data, and the orchestrator always qualifies.
- **Gated by tools.** A skill that only makes sense with certain MCP clients
  (`requires_clients`) is only offered to agents that hold one of them.

## The composer

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

CATALOG_HEADER = (
    "\n\n<available_skills>\n"
    "These skills are NOT loaded yet. Before starting any task, check whether one\n"
    "of them covers it, and call `load_skill` with its name if so. Do the work only\n"
    "after the relevant skill is loaded. If a skill you loaded earlier is no longer\n"
    "visible in your context (long runs compress old messages), load it again.\n\n"
)


@dataclass
class Skill:
    name: str
    description: str
    content: str
    strategy: str = "full"
    rules: str | None = None
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    requires_clients: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)


def compose_skills(doc: dict, skills: dict[str, Skill], active_tags: set[str]) -> None:
    for agent in doc.get("agents", {}).values():
        bound = agent.pop("skills", [])
        held = set(agent.get("mcp", []))

        def usable(skill: Skill) -> bool:
            return not skill.requires_clients or bool(held & set(skill.requires_clients))

        names = [name for name in dict.fromkeys(bound) if name in skills]
        names += [
            s.name
            for s in skills.values()
            if s.name not in names and set(s.tags) & active_tags and usable(s)
        ]

        full = [skills[n] for n in names if skills[n].strategy == "full"]
        if full:
            rules = "\n\n".join(f"### {s.name}\n{s.content}" for s in full)
            agent["system_prompt"] = (
                f'<rules priority="1">\n{rules}\n</rules>\n\n'
                f"<agent_instructions>\n{agent['system_prompt']}\n</agent_instructions>"
            )

        catalog = [
            s
            for s in skills.values()
            if (s.name in names and s.strategy != "full") or (s.name not in names and usable(s))
        ]
        if catalog:
            lines = "\n".join(f"- **{s.name}**: {s.rules or s.description}" for s in catalog)
            agent["system_prompt"] += CATALOG_HEADER + lines + "\n</available_skills>"


SKILLS = {
    "efficiency-discipline": Skill(
        "efficiency-discipline", "Avoid redundant work", "Never repeat a tool call."
    ),
    "sql-guide": Skill(
        "sql-guide", "SQL patterns", "...", strategy="rag", rules="Use when writing SQL"
    ),
    "nbo-analysis": Skill(
        "nbo-analysis", "Offer revenue analysis", "Quantify every claim.", tags=["offers"]
    ),
}

doc = {
    "agents": {
        "sql_analyst": {
            "system_prompt": "You analyse data.",
            "skills": ["efficiency-discipline"],
            "mcp": ["sql", "skills"],
        }
    }
}
compose_skills(doc, SKILLS, active_tags={"offers"})

prompt = doc["agents"]["sql_analyst"]["system_prompt"]
assert "skills" not in doc["agents"]["sql_analyst"]
assert "### efficiency-discipline" in prompt and "### nbo-analysis" in prompt
assert "- **sql-guide**: Use when writing SQL" in prompt
```

The wording of the two blocks matters. Inlined rules are framed as overriding
the agent's own instructions, so a house rule beats a workflow author's
shortcut. The catalog tells the agent to check *before* starting, to load
*before* doing the work, and to reload a skill that long-run compression has
pushed out of its context — without that last line, agents carry on from a
skill they can no longer see.

## The load tool

Agents load `catalog` and `rag` skills with one tool. Ours is a skills service
behind the MCP gateway, so every agent reaches it as `skills___load_skill` by
holding the `skills` client. A large reference skill answers a bare call with
its table of contents and asks for a query; a call with a query gets the
matching sections from a vector and keyword search.

A project without a skills service can start with a local tool over the same
catalogue:

```python
from strands import tool

LIBRARY = {
    "sql-guide": "## Joins\nPrefer explicit JOIN ... ON.\n\n## Windows\nUse ROW_NUMBER() for top-N.",
}


@tool
def load_skill(name: str, query: str | None = None) -> str:
    """Load a skill's instructions by name.

    Args:
        name: The skill to load, as listed under available skills.
        query: For a long reference skill, the topic to load sections about.
    """
    content = LIBRARY.get(name)
    if content is None:
        return f"No skill named {name!r}. Pass one of: {', '.join(sorted(LIBRARY))}."
    if query is None:
        return content
    sections = [s for s in content.split("\n\n") if query.lower() in s.lower()]
    return "\n\n".join(sections) or f"No section of {name!r} mentions {query!r}."


assert "ROW_NUMBER" in load_skill("sql-guide", "windows")
```

## Prove it

Feed the composer's output to a `Pipeline` with a scripted model, and assert on
the system prompt the model received
([Testing](../testing.md#asserting-what-the-model-was-sent)): the full skill is
inlined, the catalog lists the rest, and nothing named under `skills:` reached
the library.

# docs/recipes/structured-outputs.md

# Structured outputs a UI can render

Some results are better as a card than a paragraph: the dashboard an agent
built, an order's status, a list of findings with their sources. Give that
agent an `output_schema` and its result arrives as typed data alongside the
chat, with the schema's name telling the UI how to draw it.

## Declare the schema

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class DashboardSnippet(BaseModel):
    """Dashboard produced or updated by this agent, presented as a live card."""

    dashboard_id: str | None = Field(
        default=None,
        description="ID of the dashboard created or updated in this run. Null if none was produced.",
    )
    title: str | None = Field(default=None, description="Dashboard title.")
    summary: str | None = Field(
        default=None, description="One sentence describing what the dashboard shows."
    )


assert DashboardSnippet().dashboard_id is None
```

```yaml
agents:
  visualizer:
    output_schema: ./schemas.py:DashboardSnippet
    stream: {title: "Creating visualizations"}
```

The model reads the class docstring and every field description, so write them
for the model: say what goes in each field and what to do when there is
nothing to report. Optional fields with a `None` default let an agent that
produced nothing say so, instead of inventing an ID to satisfy the schema.

## What the client receives

The agent's `SUBAGENT_FINISHED` event carries the result:

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| `result` | The filled schema, as JSON |
| `metadata.outputSchema` | The class name, here `DashboardSnippet` |

kaboo-react keeps them on the agent's card as `structuredOutput` and
`outputSchemaName`. Register one renderer per schema name in the UI
(`structuredRenderers`); a card with no renderer for its schema shows the
result as a readable list. Keep structured output for the agents
whose result *is* a card — usually a specialist the orchestrator delegates to —
